title: DNA Structure
content:
# DNA Structure

## Learning Objectives
By the end of this lesson, you should be able to:
- Describe the structure of DNA as a double helix
- Identify the components of a nucleotide
- Explain the base pairing rules (complementary base pairing)
- Understand how the structure of DNA allows it to carry genetic information

## Introduction

**DNA** (deoxyribonucleic acid) is the molecule that carries genetic information in all living organisms. It contains the instructions needed to build and maintain an organism. The discovery of DNA's structure in 1953 by Watson and Crick (with crucial contributions from Franklin and Wilkins) is one of the most important scientific discoveries of the 20th century.

## Key Concepts

### What is DNA?

DNA is a **polymer** - a long molecule made up of many repeating units called **nucleotides**.

**Key facts about DNA:**
- Found in the nucleus of eukaryotic cells (and nucleoid of prokaryotes)
- Contains the genetic code - instructions for making proteins
- Can replicate (copy itself) before cell division
- Is inherited from parents to offspring

### The Structure of a Nucleotide

Each nucleotide consists of three parts:

1. **Phosphate group** - Contains phosphorus and oxygen
2. **Deoxyribose sugar** - A 5-carbon sugar
3. **Nitrogenous base** - One of four possible bases

[DIAGRAM: Structure of a nucleotide showing phosphate, sugar, and base]

### The Four Bases

There are four different bases in DNA:

| Base | Abbreviation | Type |
|------|--------------|------|
| Adenine | A | Purine (double ring) |
| Thymine | T | Pyrimidine (single ring) |
| Guanine | G | Purine (double ring) |
| Cytosine | C | Pyrimidine (single ring) |

**Memory aid:** "**A**pples **T**aste **G**ood, **C**ertainly" or "**A**-**T** and **G**-**C**"

### The Double Helix

DNA consists of two strands twisted around each other in a shape called a **double helix** (like a twisted ladder).

[DIAGRAM: DNA double helix showing the twisted ladder structure]

**Structure features:**

| Part | Description |
|------|-------------|
| Sugar-phosphate backbone | The "sides" of the ladder - alternating sugar and phosphate groups |
| Base pairs | The "rungs" of the ladder - bases joined by hydrogen bonds |
| Hydrogen bonds | Weak bonds holding the two strands together |
| Antiparallel strands | The two strands run in opposite directions |

### Complementary Base Pairing

The bases pair up in a specific way:

$$\text{Adenine (A)} \longleftrightarrow \text{Thymine (T)}$$
$$\text{Guanine (G)} \longleftrightarrow \text{Cytosine (C)}$$

**Base pairing rules:**
- **A always pairs with T** (2 hydrogen bonds)
- **G always pairs with C** (3 hydrogen bonds)
- A purine always pairs with a pyrimidine

This is called **complementary base pairing** because the bases complement (match) each other.

[DIAGRAM: Base pairs showing hydrogen bonds between A-T and G-C]

**Why is this important?**
1. Allows accurate DNA replication
2. One strand can act as a template for the other
3. If you know one strand's sequence, you can determine the other

### Worked Example: Complementary Sequences

**Question:** A section of one DNA strand has the sequence: A-T-G-C-C-A-T
What is the sequence of the complementary strand?

**Solution:**
Apply the base pairing rules:
- A pairs with T
- T pairs with A
- G pairs with C
- C pairs with G

| Original strand | A | T | G | C | C | A | T |
|-----------------|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Complementary | T | A | C | G | G | T | A |

**Answer:** T-A-C-G-G-T-A

### Chargaff's Rules

Before the structure was discovered, Erwin Chargaff found that in any sample of DNA:
- The amount of A equals the amount of T
- The amount of G equals the amount of C

This makes sense because of complementary base pairing!

$$\%A = \%T \text{ and } \%G = \%C$$
$$\%A + \%T + \%G + \%C = 100\%$$

**Worked example:**
If a DNA sample contains 22% adenine, calculate the percentages of the other bases.

**Solution:**
- %A = 22%, so %T = 22% (A pairs with T)
- %A + %T = 44%
- %G + %C = 100% - 44% = 56%
- %G = %C = 28% each

### DNA Replication

DNA can make exact copies of itself. This is called **DNA replication** and occurs during the S phase of the cell cycle.

**Why it works:**
- The two strands separate (hydrogen bonds break)
- Each strand acts as a template
- Free nucleotides pair up with complementary bases
- Two identical DNA molecules are produced

This is called **semi-conservative replication** because each new DNA molecule contains one original strand and one new strand.

[DIAGRAM: DNA replication showing the semi-conservative process]

### The Genetic Code

The sequence of bases in DNA forms a **code**:
- The code is read in groups of **three bases** called **codons** (or triplets)
- Each codon codes for one **amino acid**
- The sequence of codons determines the sequence of amino acids in a protein

**Example:**
```
DNA: A-T-G-C-C-A-T-T-G-G-C-A
     [ATG][CCA][TTG][GCA]
      ↓    ↓    ↓    ↓
     Met  Pro  Leu  Ala  (amino acids)
```

### How Much DNA?

| Organism | Approximate base pairs |
|----------|----------------------|
| Human | 3 billion (3 × 10⁹) |
| E. coli (bacterium) | 4.6 million |
| Fruit fly | 140 million |

Human DNA, if stretched out, would be about 2 metres long - yet it fits inside a cell nucleus about 6 μm wide!

## Historical Discovery

**Key scientists:**

| Scientist | Contribution |
|-----------|-------------|
| Rosalind Franklin | X-ray crystallography images showing helical structure |
| Maurice Wilkins | X-ray diffraction work on DNA |
| James Watson & Francis Crick | Built the first accurate model of DNA structure (1953) |
| Erwin Chargaff | Discovered base pairing ratios |

## Practical Applications

### DNA in Modern Science

1. **Forensic science:** DNA fingerprinting for crime investigation
2. **Medicine:** Genetic testing for inherited diseases
3. **Paternity testing:** Determining biological relationships
4. **Genetic engineering:** Modifying DNA for medicine and agriculture
5. **Evolutionary biology:** Comparing DNA sequences between species

## Common Exam Questions

- Describe the structure of DNA
- Explain complementary base pairing
- Calculate percentages of bases using Chargaff's rules
- Write the complementary sequence to a given strand
- Explain why DNA structure is suited to its function

## Common Misconceptions

- **Misconception:** DNA is a single strand
- **Reality:** DNA is a double helix made of two strands twisted together

- **Misconception:** A can pair with any base
- **Reality:** A only pairs with T; G only pairs with C (complementary base pairing)

- **Misconception:** DNA is only found in the nucleus
- **Reality:** DNA is also found in mitochondria and chloroplasts

- **Misconception:** The bases are connected by strong covalent bonds
- **Reality:** The bases are held together by weak hydrogen bonds (allowing the strands to separate for replication)

## Practice Questions

1. Name the four bases found in DNA. (2 marks)

2. State which base pairs with adenine. (1 mark)

3. A DNA sample contains 32% cytosine. Calculate the percentage of adenine in this sample. (2 marks)

4. A section of DNA has the base sequence: T-A-C-G-G-A-T-C-A. Write the complementary base sequence. (2 marks)

5. Describe the structure of a DNA nucleotide. (3 marks)

6. Describe the structure of DNA and explain how this structure allows DNA to replicate accurately. (6 marks)

## Key Terms Glossary

| Term | Definition |
|------|------------|
| DNA | Deoxyribonucleic acid - molecule carrying genetic information |
| Nucleotide | Monomer of DNA consisting of phosphate, sugar, and base |
| Double helix | The twisted ladder shape of DNA |
| Complementary base pairing | A pairs with T; G pairs with C |
| Hydrogen bonds | Weak bonds between base pairs |
| Phosphate-sugar backbone | The sides of the DNA ladder |
| Replication | The process of DNA copying itself |
| Semi-conservative | Each new DNA has one old and one new strand |
| Codon | Three-base sequence coding for an amino acid |
| Polymer | Large molecule made of repeating subunits |

## Summary

- DNA is a double helix made of two strands of nucleotides
- Each nucleotide contains a phosphate group, deoxyribose sugar, and a base
- The four bases are adenine (A), thymine (T), guanine (G), and cytosine (C)
- Complementary base pairing: A-T and G-C
- The strands are held together by hydrogen bonds between base pairs
- The sequence of bases forms the genetic code
- DNA can replicate semi-conservatively using complementary base pairing
